evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

spec.title: Chronic Lyme Disease Diagnostic Delay and Care-Access Barriers (2009-2010 U.S. Patient Survey)
spec.boundary: This simulation reproduces percentage-based findings from a 2011 peer-reviewed web-based survey of 2,424 U.S. residents with clinically diagnosed, lab-confirmed chronic Lyme disease (symptoms persisting 6+ months despite at least 21 days of antibiotics), surveyed June 2009-March 2010. It covers diagnostic delay, travel burden, hospital-access difficulty, and insurance/disability benefit denial rates as reported by respondents. It does not include any dollar cost figures computed by this study (the study itself collected no cost data), does not include the CDC case-count/underreporting discussion, and does not break any finding down by age, sex/gender, socioeconomic status, or race/ethnicity because the authors did not collect or analyze those variables. The sample is self-selected, internet-recruited, and limited to chronic/persistent-symptom patients, excluding early or acute Lyme disease by design.

takeaway.patient: In this self-selected online survey of people already diagnosed with chronic Lyme disease, the study reported that many respondents experienced long diagnostic delays, substantial travel for treatment, difficulty getting hospital care, and frequent denial of new insurance coverage or disability benefits linked to one medical society's contested Lyme treatment guidelines. These are patterns the study found in its own sample, not a prediction about any individual's own experience.
takeaway.care: Among this patient-reported sample, a large share described seeing 10 or more physicians before diagnosis, difficulty obtaining local hospital treatment, and barriers tied to clinical guideline disputes - including hospitals reportedly restricting privileges for physicians who do not follow one society's guidelines and insurers requiring a specialist consult before covering treatment. These findings describe patient-reported experience with care pathways and credentialing/coverage policy, not a measured outcome of any specific care team's own practice.
takeaway.policy: The study found that, within applicant subgroups, substantial shares of chronic Lyme disease patients reported denial of new insurance coverage and denial of disability benefits specifically for non-conformity with one medical society's treatment guidelines, alongside reports that hospital credentialing and insurer coverage criteria were tied to the same guidelines. This suggests clinical guideline disputes can translate into measurable coverage and benefit-access friction in this patient-reported sample, though the sample is self-selected and chronic-illness-only, so population-level generalization requires caution.

patient: If pursuing a Lyme disease diagnosis or treatment, consider asking a clinician how they approach differing Lyme treatment guidelines, since the study found guideline disputes were associated with hospital-access and benefit-denial difficulties for some patients.

Before applying for new health insurance or disability benefits after a Lyme diagnosis, consider gathering documentation of lab-confirmed diagnosis and treatment history in advance, since the study reported substantial denial rates among applicants in its sample.

If facing long travel for treatment, connecting with Lyme-focused patient advocacy organizations may help identify closer care options, since the study found travel burden was common among its respondents.

These figures describe one self-selected survey sample with chronic symptoms; a person's own experience may differ, and the study did not assess how results vary by age, sex, or other personal characteristics.
care: Reviewing local hospital credentialing and privileging policies for how they treat adherence to contested Lyme treatment guidelines may be worth checking against this study's finding that such policies restricted some physicians' treatment options.

Examining current referral patterns for suspected chronic Lyme disease cases against this study's reported diagnostic-delay pattern (many respondents reporting 7 or more physicians seen before diagnosis) could help identify where care coordination gaps arise.
Tracking emergency-department utilization among patients with persistent Lyme-related symptoms may be useful, given the study's finding that over half of respondents reported at least one such visit.
Any protocol changes should account for this being a self-selected, chronic-illness-only patient sample without demographic breakdowns, not a representative clinical audit.
policy: Reviewing how insurer medical-necessity criteria and disability-determination criteria reference specific clinical practice guidelines could help clarify whether guideline disputes are functioning as de facto coverage policy, as this study's respondents reported.

Commissioning or supporting a more representative, randomly sampled study of Lyme disease healthcare access and benefit denial - ideally with age, sex, and socioeconomic breakdowns - could help confirm whether these patterns generalize beyond this self-selected chronic-illness sample.

When evaluating disability or insurance appeals processes, consider whether denial reasons tied to guideline non-conformity are being tracked and reviewed, since the study reported this as a specific denial rationale among applicants in its sample.
Any policy use of these percentages should separately account for the study's own limitation that it cannot be generalized to early/acute Lyme disease patients, who were excluded by design.

package.documentation:
This simulator uses percentage-based findings from a 2011 peer-reviewed study (Health Policy) reporting a web-based survey of 2,424 U.S. residents with clinically diagnosed, lab-confirmed chronic Lyme disease (symptoms persisting 6+ months despite at least 21 days of antibiotics), surveyed June 2009-March 2010. All inputs and outputs are observed survey percentages from Table 2 (p.68) and Table 3 (p.69); none are dollar costs, since this study did not collect cost data itself (it only cites an external 2006 cost-of-illness study, Zhang et al., for context - $1,310/year early-stage and $16,199/year late-stage Lyme disease, a different population and price year, not reproduced here).

Inputs cover diagnostic delay (share seeing 10+ physicians before diagnosis), travel burden (share traveling over 50 miles for treatment), hospital-access difficulty (among those who sought local hospital care), insurance-coverage denial and disability-benefit denial (each among their own applicant subgroups), and emergency-room utilization. The insurance-versus-disability denial gap output is a constructed, illustrative comparison between two subgroup-specific denial rates reported separately in the document; the document itself does not compute this gap.

Limitations: This pooled sample has not been broken down by age, sex/gender, socioeconomic status, or race/ethnicity - the authors explicitly state these variables were not assessed in their survey, though federal survey data sources such as NHIS and BRFSS generally support disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform one. The study also describes a systemic limitation distinct from the accuracy of these percentages: it reports that one medical society's Lyme treatment guidelines function as de facto enforced policy - hospitals reportedly restrict privileges for physicians not following these guidelines, insurers reportedly require a specialist consultation before covering treatment, and disability benefits are reportedly denied for guideline non-conformity - creating a barrier to care independent of individual clinical presentation.

The sample is self-selected and internet-recruited, limited to patients with chronic/persistent symptoms, and explicitly excludes early or acute Lyme disease patients by the authors' own design, so findings should not be generalized to the full spectrum of Lyme disease patients.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- CDC-reported new Lyme disease cases, 2008 (2008, the United States): the document reports 35,198; CDC's reported cases were 35,198 (confirmed and probable together), so the document's figure is within 10% of the CDC confirmed-plus-probable total (+0.0% versus the total). Definitions may differ between the document and CDC surveillance, so a gap is a prompt to check, not an error. Federal source: public health surveillance (surveillance report), 2008-2021; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- CDC-acknowledged estimated annual Lyme disease cases (low bound, ~6x reported) (2008, the United States): the document's estimate of 200,000 is 5.7 times the 35,198 cases CDC received as reported. Reported cases are a passive-surveillance subset, so estimates from claims or models are usually higher; this shows the size of the gap, not which figure is right. Federal source: public health surveillance (surveillance report), 2008-2021; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- CDC-acknowledged estimated annual Lyme disease cases (high bound, ~12x reported) (2008, the United States): the document's estimate of 400,000 is 11.4 times the 35,198 cases CDC received as reported. Reported cases are a passive-surveillance subset, so estimates from claims or models are usually higher; this shows the size of the gap, not which figure is right. Federal source: public health surveillance (surveillance report), 2008-2021; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Mean annual cost of illness, early Lyme disease (cited from Zhang et al. 2006): 1,310.00 in 2006 dollars is about 2,091.99 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.597). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Mean annual cost of illness, late Lyme disease (cited from Zhang et al. 2006): 16,199.00 in 2006 dollars is about 25,868.82 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.597). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
